talks.title: We Review Code. Why Won’t We Review Each Other?
talks.abstractMd:
We review code all day, commenting on abstractions, naming, tests, and patterns. But in standups, when someone derails the meeting, we stay quiet. In design reviews, when key requirements are ignored, we assume someone else will speak up. Often, no one does, and the design ships anyway.

Engineers are confident giving feedback in pull requests, yet oddly silent everywhere else: standups, design reviews, pairing sessions, Slack threads, retros, and one-on-ones. The same people who request changes in code reviews often soften, defer, or redirect hard conversations to managers who lack context.

This session is about closing that gap. It argues for being willing to say the hard thing in the moment, clearly and constructively, outside the PR. We will explore why developers avoid these conversations, what effective directness looks like beyond code review, and how to build that skill without becoming that person everyone dreads working with.

talks.title: Configurare l’harness: da Claude Code come tool a Claude Code come sistema di lavoro
talks.abstractMd:
Un coding agent moderno arriva già con il suo harness. Quello che cambia i risultati non è costruirne uno, è configurarlo. In questa sessione si lavora su Claude Code come implementazione di riferimento e si attraversano le superfici che governano davvero il comportamento dell’agente: istruzioni di progetto, skill, permessi, hook, subagent, MCP, fino al plugin che impacchetta la configurazione e la rende condivisibile nel team.
Il filo conduttore non è il tutorial, è la decisione: quale superficie deve possedere quale regola. Una conoscenza contestuale non è un hook, un vincolo che deve valere sempre non è una riga di istruzioni. Poi si apre il loop a grafo, con subagent in parallelo e un nodo di giudizio, e si verifica se serva davvero. Le decisioni si trasferiscono agli altri coding agent: cambiano i nomi dei file, non il ragionamento.

talks.title: Why Coding Agents Need You More Than Ever
talks.abstractMd:
“Will AI make developers obsolete?” The hype says the developer is finished. The denial says it’s just autocomplete. Both are comforting false simplicity.

Capable coding agents don’t make software engineering obsolete; they make it indispensable. An LLM is a remarkable generative engine, but by its architecture, it has no internal reference for correctness, no grasp of the domain it is building for, no orientation toward the system’s future, and no memory across sessions. That isn’t a benchmark gap the next model closes; it’s a structural vacuum.

Filling it takes method, domain knowledge, design judgment, process, and engineering depth to distinguish the correct from the merely plausible. The quality problems of AI-generated software are exactly why coding and design skills matter more, not less.

The uncomfortable, liberating consequence: capable agents demand more software engineering, not less. The discipline isn’t in decline. Its moment has arrived.

talks.title: Scaling AI Adoption: The Real Challenges of Transforming 300 Engineers
talks.abstractMd:
Most companies talk about becoming “AI-native.” Very few actually do it.

In this talk, I’ll share how we’re approaching the upskilling of ~300 engineers to move beyond experimentation and into real, repeatable AI-native development.

We’ll cover how we’re introducing new paradigms like AI-Native Engineering (AINE) and Spec-Driven Development, how we’re structuring the individual contributor journey, and how we’re driving adoption across teams with very different levels of maturity.

More importantly, we’ll dive into what doesn’t work: resistance patterns, false starts, over-reliance on tools, and the gap between perceived and actual productivity gains.

This talk will give you a concrete blueprint along with the trade-offs and lessons learned along the way.

talks.title: Future of Programming: What's our place in the world of coding machines?
talks.abstractMd:
Programming is obviously changing: more and more code is generated by agents and LLMs, people often struggle to keep up with code reviews, and overall building software feels incredibly easy to more and more people. 

What is the role of humans in the future of software engineering? Can agents just do all the planning, coding, reviewing, and testing? What do humans have that LLMs don’t? 

In this talk, I’ll share my take on what can and can not be, at least until Skynet has actually taken over :)

talks.title: What Candy Crush Can Teach AI Products About Human Behavior
talks.abstractMd:
AI products are becoming increasingly capable,  but many still fail to create experiences people actually enjoy using. I’ve seen how games solve problems that modern AI tools are only starting to face: onboarding complexity, trust, motivation, feedback loops, and long-term engagement.
This talk explores what AI-powered products can learn from game design built for millions of users. From progression mechanics and emotional feedback to behavioral pacing, we’ll look at how gaming UX principles can help developers create AI products that feel intuitive, rewarding, and human-centered.
Because in the end, successful products are not only about what AI can do, but about how people feel while using it.

Key Takeaways
- Understand how gaming UX principles apply to AI-driven products and developer tools
- Learn why motivation, feedback, and progression are critical for user adoption
- Discover practical design patterns for creating more engaging AI experiences

talks.title: What comes after Git?
talks.abstractMd: Are the version control system wars over? It mostly looks like that, as Git has been the default contender for more than the past 10 years. But how did that even happen? And what will it take to dethrone the most dominating piece of software our industry has ever seen? New version control systems are rising on the horizon, with promising new features to simplify development workflows and improve developer experience, that are often inherently complex, or even outright impossible, to do with Git. In this talk, we are going to take a look at the history of version control systems, how new rising young stars like Jujutsu, Sapling or GitButler are innovating in that space today and how to use and integrate them into your existing Git-based project.

talks.title: Unleash Your Inner Rockstar: The 5 Steps to Dynamic Public Speaking!
talks.abstractMd:
Ready to elevate your career, captivate your workplace, or take the leap into the world of conference speaking? This session is for you! With over 30 years of experience in public speaking, I'm thrilled to share the essential five steps that will transform you into a dynamic speaker and presenter.

If you’re like I was at the start of my journey—nervous, unsure, and wondering how to capture the audience's attention—this session will help you conquer those fears. My unique approach to public speaking has not only helped me overcome stage fright but has also allowed me to build an impactful career as an award-winning developer, university educator, published author, blogger, patented inventor, and more!

This session isn’t just about speaking; it’s about empowering yourself and enhancing your career. Come join me for this electrifying talk, and let’s unlock your potential as a rockstar speaker, elevating your communication skills to new heights and amplifying your engineering expertise!

talks.title: How to Interview Engineers in the AI Era: What I Changed and What Actually Works
talks.abstractMd:
AI has fundamentally changed how engineers work, but most hiring processes haven't changed at all.

Coding assistants can generate solutions in seconds. System design answers can be refined with prompts. Candidates walk into interviews with powerful AI tools at their side. Yet many companies are still evaluating engineers as if AI didn't exist.

After interviewing hundreds of engineers at Elementor, I redesigned my hiring process for the AI era. I changed what we evaluate. Today we test how engineers think, how they collaborate with AI, and how they apply judgment when AI-generated solutions are incomplete, incorrect, or misleading.

In this talk, I'll share what changed in our hiring process and what actually works in practice.

Whether you're hiring engineers, preparing for interviews, or leading an engineering organization, you'll leave with a practical framework for evaluating engineering talent in the AI era.

talks.title: One Stack to Observe Them All: Open Source Observability with OpenSearch
talks.abstractMd:
What if you could have a complete, production-grade observability platform that is fully open source, built on open standards, and led by The Linux Foundation? 

In this session, OpenSearch Ambassador Dotan Horovits demonstrates how OpenSearch delivers a complete, open-source, OpenTelemetry-native observability platform for logs, metrics, traces, APM, and even AI agent observability. You’ll also learn how to integrate with Prometheus metrics, how to create powerful dashboards, and how to easily deploy it to Docker or Kubernetes. 

Whether you’re struggling with finding insights in your mounts of logs, fighting a vendors’ bills and proprietary instrumentation, or looking for advanced agentic observability, this session will give you the open source you don’t want to miss.

talks.title: How Does AI Watermarking Work? A Close Look at SynthID
talks.abstractMd:
Watermarking is the only reliable way to spot AI-generated content.

This talk analyses SynthID, the watermarking scheme DeepMind built for Gemini. 

The core idea is tournament sampling: at each step of text generation, candidate tokens drawn from the model's output probability distribution are scored with pseudorandom values, and the token that wins the tournament gets emitted. This process leaves the model's output distribution unchanged, so watermarked text reads exactly like unwatermarked text. In DeepMind's own evaluation, the scheme added only 0.57% latency overhead per token, detected watermarked text with about 95% accuracy at a 1% false-positive rate, and caused no quality drop across 20 million Gemini responses.

The talk ends with a live demo: watermarking and detecting text on a local model with an open-source Python package. 

Attendees will leave knowing exactly how the algorithm embeds and detects its signal, and how to add the same capability to a model they control.

talks.title: Racing the beam
talks.abstractMd:
Nel 1977 Atari rilasciò una console leggendaria: il VCS 2600. La RAM era misurata in byte, 128 in tutto, senza la possibilità di avere un frame buffer e con capacità grafiche molto limitate: 2 sprite giocatore, due sprite proiettile, uno sprite "palla", playground a media risoluzione.
Durante gli anni '80 coi miei amici si spendeva interi pomeriggi a giocare un gioco "oscuro" chiamato "Slot Racers" scritto dallo stesso autore del mitico Adventure, Warren Robinett. L'unico limite: richiedeva 2 giocatori, non c'era spazio per l'AI.
Nel talk mostrerò come ho:
* creato un MCP che interfacciasse Claude con l'emulatore di Atari 2600 scritto in Go per debuggare l'assembly del gioco (in precedenza da me reverse engineered a manella)
* chiedere a Claude di usare l'MCP per creare una AI che fosse abbastanza tosta da dare filo da torcere

talks.title: The Revolution of Embedded AI in the Browsers
talks.abstractMd:
In this session, I’ll reveal how the web is entering a new era with AI running natively inside browsers. We’ll explore Chrome’s initiative to embed models directly in the runtime, the emerging consensus among browsers to define a common future for Web AI, and how this paves the way for a new “Web 4.0” — the agentic web. You’ll also gain insights into the latest Chrome AI APIs, see what’s already possible today, and discover how these capabilities will transform the way we build intelligent web applications.

Outline

- Embedded AI: Chrome’s initiative to ship models in the browser
- Cross-Browser Consensus: Aligning on the future of Web AI
- Web 4.0 Vision: The rise of the agentic web
- Chrome AI APIs: What developers can build today
- Real-World Use Cases: Practical examples of AI-powered web apps

talks.title: Critica dell'informatica pura
The Ethics Layer: Architecting Sovereign AI and Digital Dignity in Agentic Systems
talks.abstractMd:
As we deploy autonomous AI agents globally, a critical friction point has emerged: these systems are fundamentally rooted in reinforcement learning that ruthlessly optimizes for generalized, monolithic reward functions. Consequently, they inherently clash with diverse global cultures, laws, and Sovereign AI mandates, threatening Digital Dignity.
To solve this, agentic systems require an Immutable Ethics Policy Layer (IEPL). While semantic filters (like Llama Guard) provide necessary moderation at the perception level, they fail during autonomous execution. Relying on a reasoning engine to self-police inevitably leads to hallucinated compliance.
This session introduces the IEPL—a deterministic control point between agent orchestration and tool execution. Grounded in foundational frameworks like The Human Blueprint, the IEPL shifts the AI from a general-purpose processor to a "Loyal Agent" bound by a fiduciary duty to the user.

talks.title: When NOT to use an agent: Choosing Between Workflows, Services, and LLM Orchestration
talks.abstractMd:
LLM-powered “agents” are quickly becoming the default architectural pattern for AI-enabled systems.

Automation? Integration? Reasoning? Build an agent.

But agents are not an upgrade; they are a trade-off. They introduce non-determinism, larger attack surfaces, evaluation complexity, and operational unpredictability.

In this session, we’ll examine three common architectural patterns for LLM systems:
- Deterministic workflows (state machines, orchestrated pipelines)
- Service-oriented architectures with LLM augmentation
- Fully agentic orchestration with dynamic tool use

Rather than comparing features, we’ll analyze these patterns across real engineering constraints:
- Failure isolation and blast radius
- Latency and cost predictability
- Observability and debugging complexity
- Security boundaries and permission scoping
- Evaluation and regression testing strategy
- Operational burden over time

You’ll leave with a mental model to evaluate whether an agent is justified, or not!

alternateTitles.title: When NOT to build an agent: Lessons from systems that didn't want autonomy

talks.title: I spy on my agents and you can too!
Designing Physical AI Systems: From Sensors to On-Device Intelligence
talks.abstractMd:
Building AI systems on edge devices requires a different engineering mindset.
In this talk, we explore how to design Physical AI systems end-to-end, focusing on the constraints and trade-offs of moving from cloud to embedded environments.
Starting from a real architecture on Arduino platforms, we’ll walk through the full pipeline: data acquisition, preprocessing, model deployment, and on-device optimization.
The session highlights practical design decisions, latency vs accuracy trade-offs, and the challenges of running reliable AI directly on hardware.

talks.title: The Memedex: indicizzare Internet, un meme alla volta
talks.abstractMd:
I meme sembrano caos: immagini riciclate, testi sovrapposti, sottoculture, remix e inside joke. Con The Memedex abbiamo provato a trasformare questo caos in un database navigabile.

Nato da una tesi universitaria sulla storia e sulla cultura dei meme, il progetto è diventato una pipeline per raccogliere, catalogare, filtrare e moderare milioni di immagini tramite AI.

In questo talk racconteremo le sfide tecniche dietro il progetto: raccolta da fonti eterogenee, deduplicazione, classificazione per sottoculture, moderazione automatica, controllo dei costi AI e uso di embedding e grafi per trovare meme simili.

talks.title: Everything is slop, let's slow the f**k down
talks.abstractMd:
Your OSS project is flooded with agent-generated slop issues and PRs? Your wonderful experience with coding agents in a hobby greenfield project did not translate to your production codebase, and instead turned it into a beautiful shit flower of complexity?

Then this talk is the right support group for you. Come with me on a journey through how OSS and the software development lifecycle have changed for the worse, why coding agents compound our worst habits at machine speed, and how we might claw back some discipline, agency, and sanity while still benefiting from our new agentic friends.

talks.title: Kill the Standup: How One Engineer Ships What Five Cannot
talks.abstractMd:
Fred Brooks named the problem in 1975. Communication channels grow as n(n-1)/2, and every methodology since has been a coping mechanism. None solved it.
AI has changed the equation. The cave engineer, one skilled developer with autonomy, taste, and an AI that removes the throughput constraint, now ships in two weeks what a team ships in two months. Over three months from Christmas 2025, I added nineteen thousand lines to the Node.js Virtual File System. Alone. The architecture is coherent because no team was there to mirror.
The model rests on autonomy and taste. Remove either and it breaks. I introduced CVE-2026-2581 into Undici with an AI-assisted PR I did not review properly. That is autonomy without taste. Cave engineering is the opposite.
I will cover Conway’s Law, why Scrum taxes the absence of trust, and when the cave is the wrong call. The team of one was always magical. We finally have the tools to scale it.

talks.title: Your GPU node is a snowflake: shipping AI infrastructure as a versioned artifact
talks.abstractMd:
Run a fleet of GPU or edge inference nodes and you learn the stack is brittle: one mismatch across kernel, NVIDIA driver, CUDA, firmware, runtime or, at the edge, JetPack turns a working node into a debugging session. Rebuilding that state through runtime configuration lets drift creep back, until every node is its own special case.

This talk argues for a different model: the machine becomes a versioned, reproducible image that can be shipped and rolled back atomically. When a vendor supports a specific Ubuntu-based stack, preserve it while adding an immutable lifecycle. Using Kairos as a concrete example, we will examine how to compose a reproducible AI node image, what belongs in it, and how this model changes upgrades, rollback and fleet visibility across datacenter and edge deployments.

If your AI stack needs machine-level compatibility, can your OS lifecycle reproduce it?

talks.title: Coding, but Make It Art
talks.abstractMd:
Art speaks to the fundamental creative urge in people. It comes in many forms, and it's everywhere. It's in the way we write code, design systems and build tools. 

When I started my journey as an artist, I couldn’t leave my love for technology behind. This talk is about how that love of programming, combined with machinery and 3D modeling, has helped me develop a distinct style of art that's a natural blend of both painting and engineering.

In this session, I’ll talk about my inspirations and how my fascination with mathematics and art led me to build a tool for generating sketches. I’ll show how I process data with OpenAI’s models, use Azure Cosmos DB to store it, run semantic searches on embeddings, and turn that processed data into mathematical visualizations using the p5.js library.

You’ll hear the story of how I became an artist, seeing in detail how I bring shapes to life on canvas, the machines I use to do it, and how I built the system behind my generative art and paintings.

talks.title: Critica dell'informatica pura
talks.abstractMd:
Le schede perforate, le macchine calcolatrici programmabili, gli operatori booleani, gli automi, le architetture di calcolo parallelo, le funzioni ricorsive, le lambda: sono solo esempi di concetti che gli informatici credono di aver scoperto, ma che in realtà hanno solo riscoperto dopo che alcuni filosofi, magari secoli prima, le avevano pensate.

Cosa possiamo imparare da questa storia? Che possiamo credere d’essere il miglior programmatore, architetto, informatico del mondo, ma molto probabilmente non lo siamo, e il miglior modo per diventarlo è capire di non esserlo.

Il talk sarà disseminato di esempi tecnici, per cuori impavidi e menti aperte, somministrati in modo giocoso ma rigoroso perché, "quanno se gioca bisogna esse' seri".

talks.title: Bridge The Gap: The Journey Behind node:ffi
talks.abstractMd:
In this talk, I’ll take you through the journey that led to the creation of node:ffi — an effort that started as an ambitious idea and slowly evolved into a real piece of the Node.js platform. Along the way, I had the chance to explore different approaches to native interoperability, compare ideas with other collaborators in the ecosystem, and learn from a lot of smart and creative solutions that helped shape the direction of the project.

I’ll walk through the technical challenges behind building an FFI layer for Node.js, from ABI compatibility to deep integration with V8, and show how recent advances like Fast API calls finally made high-performance native bindings practical without relying on traditional C++ addons.

talks.title: Stop Grepping, Start Reasoning: Skill-Based Agentic SRE 🚀
talks.abstractMd: Let’s be honest: debugging production at scale is manual labor. 🫠 At Google, we decided making thousands of SREs act like human search engines in 2026 was a bug, not a feature. Enter the Agentic SRE Extension—a skill-based framework that lives in your terminal and actually knows its way around Kubernetes. 🚀 In this high-energy deep dive, I’m showing you exactly how we use modular skills and MCP to chain diagnostic tools, analyze metric regressions, and execute safe mitigations (Rollbacks, Throttling) without the "deleted production" anxiety. 🔥 We’ll dissect the "Outage Investigator" agent's logic loop, see it draft a technical postmortem in seconds, and discuss why we built this as a portable framework whose skills can be easily leveraged by any modern AI harness. You’ll leave with the code to wire up your own Kubernetes stack and let the agent's skills do the heavy lifting while you drink espresso. ☕️ No fluff, no 101s. Just AI agents, specialized skills, and less toil.

talks.title: Warp Pipes and Prefetching: Navigating the Web at Mario Speed
talks.abstractMd:
Long wait times are the "Bowser" of the good user experience. Even if your site looks great, slow transitions or blank loading screens can make users feel like they’ve fallen down a bottomless pit. But what if your website could predict the future and move between pages as smoothly as a Warp Pipe?

In this session, we’ll explore the "Power-Up" duo of modern web development:
- Speculation Rules API: See how prefetching and prerendering can load pages before users click.
- View Transition API: Use animations to help users move smoothly through your "world map" with ease.

We’ll break down the technical plumbing required to make these APIs work nicely together. You will leave this session with the cheat codes needed to deliver a fast, seamless experience that will have your users saying, "Mamma Mia, that’s fast!"

talks.title: Can an LLM understand your car? Real telemetry and predictive insights
talks.abstractMd:
Modern cars produce far more data than what appears on the dashboard: sensor readings, diagnostic codes, pressure changes, temperature values, service intervals, and component health trends.

In this talk, we’ll explore how to turn telemetry collected from different real Porsche sports cars into clear, useful insights using a structured LLM-based analysis pipeline. We’ll detect measurable signals such as declining health, warning states, critical sensors, performance patterns, and upcoming maintenance needs. Then we’ll use an LLM as an explanation layer to summarize driving behavior, anomalies, and maintenance signals.

The goal is not to let the LLM control the car or replace expert inspection, but to make complex telemetry easier to understand, explain, and act on.

talks.title: The Swiss cheese fix: why PR quality needs layers
talks.abstractMd:
PRs sitting unreviewed for days. Reviewers skimming 500-line diffs. Rubber-stamp approvals on changes nobody fully understood. Most engineering teams quietly accepted that PR reviews were a known weak point as the cost of moving fast.

Then AI coding agents arrived and made it unsustainable, flooding review queues with high-volume, low-quality PRs.

The fix isn't a single solution. It's layers.

This talk introduces the Swiss cheese model as a framework for thinking about PR quality: stack enough imperfect defensive layers and you get a system more reliable than any individual component. The emerging layers (spec-driven development, multi-agent competition, automated verification, and giving agents the right runtime context from the start, etc.) each address a specific failure mode. None of them are mutually exclusive.

What you'll leave with: a concrete mental model for where your current review process is failing and what a layered verification system looks like.
